extracted.intended_audience: aspiring journalists, young newspaper editors, and those planning or managing newspaper operations
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and editorial guidance for producing a newspaper: choosing audience and editorial stance, staffing and education of journalists, adopting printing technologies and production practices, and managing the economics of a newspaper business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of news agencies (United Press) to supply world news
rubrics_metrics.description: The system known as the United Press supplies the news of the whole world so the individual editor need only look after the news of his own locality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies have revolutionized the profession by doing the news-getting drudgery; this frees editors to devote themselves to the intellectual part of the business and to produce more thoughtful, higher-quality papers. Editors should rely on such associations to obtain timely international and national reports rather than attempting to hunt every item themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide target audience (for sensible people or for fools)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before making a paper ask: will you make a newspaper for sensible people, or will you make a newspaper for fools?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both are valid commercial choices — papers aimed at less discerning readers can be profitable — but editors should consciously choose which audience they serve and shape content accordingly. Author prefers newspapers that try to serve intelligent readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include comprehensive panorama of recent events
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper should present to the reader a panorama of all the events of the preceding day — local, national, and international.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage telegraph and agency content to give readers a concise history of the globe's events daily; readers expect to learn what happened elsewhere (e.g., France, Turkey, Persia) as part of their morning paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence from party
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper must be independent of its party or it fails to be the ideal newspaper; the editor should manifest independence when the party departs from principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should know and state their principles clearly, and be prepared to criticize their own party when warranted. Faithfulness to principle and a willingness to break with party lines are valued (examples: Horace Greeley).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and faithfulness in expressing principles
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be faithfulness and a clear declaration of the newspaper's principles so readers know where it stands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor, as public guide, must have a power of determination and intelligence; express principles explicitly rather than hiding or equivocating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly and linguistic education for journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: A young journalist should learn everything possible, including a strict classical education (Greek and Latin) and, above all, thorough mastery of the English language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deep familiarity with language and classical texts lets an editor write and edit without error or ambiguity. Knowing English thoroughly prevents saying what is not meant; examples and anecdotes illustrate consequences of weak language knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical scientific and legal knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should know practical sciences (especially chemistry and electricity), history (particularly American history), the American Constitution, and constitutional law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These subjects enable accurate reporting and informed commentary on technical and civic matters; political economy is noted but treated with less emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of content: not only petty local news but literary/scientific articles
rubrics_metrics.description: With agency-provided routine news, papers should include correspondence, literary, scientific, or romantic articles to make the paper more interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associative arrangements freeing editors from petty reporting allow newspapers to improve intellectual content and variety, attracting better-educated readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report crimes and sensational events (newsworthiness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers are a picture of the world and must report crimes, swindles, forgeries, and murders because they arrest public attention and readers expect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempting to suppress such news would drive readers to other papers; editors may report disturbing facts without moral objection if events occurred and are of public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt modern printing presses and equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern presses (e.g., Hoe presses) can print, fold, count, and deliver tens of thousands of finished papers per hour, producing large editions efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in high-capacity, mechanized presses to ensure speed, accuracy (machine folding/counting eliminates mistakes), and the ability to serve dealers without manual counting; these machines are a revolution in operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt mechanical typesetting (Linotype/Mergenthaler) while weighing typographical quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical typesetters (Mergenthaler/Linotype) set type by keyboard and cast slugs, significantly reducing typesetting cost (often to half of hand-setting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While cheaper, machine-set pages may be less typographically handsome than hand-set type. Publishers should weigh cost savings against aesthetic/typographical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stereotype plates and photographic/zinc plates for efficient illustration reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: No types are put upon the press; stereotyped plates of whole pages are used; photographic processes on prepared zinc plates allow cheap and fast reproduction of portraits and illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modern photographic etching to zinc reduces illustration cost dramatically (example: portrait costing $40–50 previously can cost $1.25 now). Implement these technologies to expand illustrated content affordably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure cheap, reliable paper supplies (wood pulp)
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper production moved from rags to rye straw to wood pulp; modern printing paper is now made from soft wood (spruce/pine) pulp, drastically reducing cost to about two and a quarter cents a pound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decline in paper cost is a major factor making large editions profitable. Editors should source pulp-based paper and understand supply economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand capital and fixed-cost requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Running a large newspaper requires substantial capital — stated minimum about one million dollars — to buy presses (four big presses at roughly $45,000 each), electric lighting, dynamos, and other plant equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper capitalization is necessary to run the enterprise at reasonable cost and avoid being overwhelmed by expenses. New entrants must budget for heavy upfront investment beyond normal operating costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use electricity and proper plant engineering (lighting and power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Electric lighting and plant power (dynamo driven by steam engine powering presses and lights) are indispensable and preferable to gas because they avoid excessive heat and hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Install electric lighting and integrate dynamos with press steam power; though installation costs are large, operating conditions (especially in summer) are vastly improved and safer for staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanized finishing and distribution reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern presses fold, count, and stack papers so dealers receive piles ready for sale without manual counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanized handling reduces human counting errors and distribution disputes; prioritize equipment that automates finishing tasks for operational reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing: hire better-educated, capable people and value women reporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of mechanization and agencies fewer men are employed but they tend to be better educated and more capable; women are increasingly employed as reporters, writers, and artists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer competitive salaries (which have generally risen) and utilize diverse talent; be aware of staff turnover patterns (author notes women often leave upon marriage) and plan retention accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial viability: price vs cost calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the relationship between paper cost, printing cost, sale price (retail and wholesale), and profit; example: paper cost and Tribunes' pricing figures are given to show margins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate per-pound paper yields and edition sizes to estimate profitability; use mechanization and cheap paper to keep per-copy cost low while covering salaries, news-gathering, and rents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate moral/social questions (e.g., Sunday paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to make a Sunday newspaper raises moral and social duty questions; public demand largely decides their existence, and the author does not find making or reading Sunday papers morally objectionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both market demand and personal/conscience views; if the public will buy, Sunday papers will be made; editors should weigh ethical considerations but recognize commercial realities.
